slides: Open by contrasting coordinate movement with distribution movement. Ordinary gradient descent measures steps in the visible parameter coordinates, while natural gradient uses the Fisher metric to measure how far the model distribution moves. Singular learning then asks what happens when that metric loses rank.

This slide is the conceptual hinge. The ordinary gradient is steepest only for Euclidean unit balls. Once the Fisher metric defines the unit ball, the natural direction solves a constrained steepest-descent problem, and the ellipse figure shows why equal screen length is not equal statistical length.

The trajectory comparison gives the payoff in a well-conditioned local model. Euclidean descent follows narrow contours and must respect the stiff direction, while natural gradient rescales by the metric. The check confirms both paths are monotone and the natural final loss is lower.

Use this slide to connect natural gradient with neighboring algorithms. Stochastic relaxation, policy gradients, online estimation, and saturated neural units all share the same question: what is the behavior-level direction after the metric decides which coordinate moves are large or small?

The Hessian slide prevents an over-simple story. Newton-like scaling is powerful near minima, but an indefinite Hessian at a saddle can point toward a bad stabilizing direction. Replacing eigenvalues by absolute values keeps curvature scaling while encouraging escape along negative curvature.

Mirror descent should be presented as the dual-coordinate cousin of natural gradient. Negative entropy creates log-ratio coordinates where the step looks Euclidean, while the primal path stays on the simplex. The checks verify positivity, normalization, and monotone objective decrease.

Singular regions are the second half of the chapter. In the one-hidden-unit model, axes of unidentifiability collapse Fisher eigenvalues because changing one parameter no longer changes the output behavior. The heatmap makes metric rank loss visible rather than purely formal.

The plateau slide connects singular geometry to learning dynamics. Ordinary gradient can spend hundreds of iterations near a collapsed region, while the natural-gradient behavior-space direction reaches the threshold much faster. The prior-mass panel warns that singular regions also distort statistical asymptotics.

The damping lab adds practical caution. A nearly singular Fisher matrix can produce enormous raw natural-gradient steps, so implementations solve a damped system instead. The figure and rows show the tradeoff: damping reduces step norm, but too much damping erases useful metric correction.

Close with the validation story. The chapter checks metric positive definiteness where expected, monotone descent, Fisher eigenvalue collapse on singular axes, plateau slowdown, damping tradeoffs, and artifact integrity. The lesson is not that natural gradient removes singularities, but that it exposes their geometry.
